title: 'I Like My Big Rat Wife': Meet the People Using Chatbots to Write Custom Fiction
gist: A University of Washington study analyzing over 500,000 WildChat ChatGPT prompts found more than a third involve fiction/role-play generation, driven by a small group of obsessive 'power users,' with researchers suggesting AI's unpredictability, judgment-free nature, and infinite iteration are creating a durable new mode of personal, on-demand storytelling and erotica that could reshape publishing into a tiered system.

themes.theme: Scale of AI fiction usage among chatbot users

insights.claim: A University of Washington study analyzing more than 500,000 prompts from the public WildChat ChatGPT dataset found that over a third of chatbot interactions involve some form of fiction generation, including prose, poetry, fan fiction, erotica, or role-play.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: A third of chatbot usage being fiction/role-play-related suggests entertainment and companionship use cases are a much larger share of consumer LLM demand than commonly assumed, relevant to product strategy and monetization for consumer AI apps.
insights.quote: Analyzing more than 500,000 prompts fed into ChatGPT, drawn from a public dataset called WildChat, the researchers found that more than a third of chatbot interactions involve some form of fiction generation.

insights.claim: The vast majority of fiction-generation activity in the WildChat dataset comes from a small group of obsessive 'power users'; in one extreme case, a single user prompted ChatGPT to regenerate variations of the same Doki Doki Literature Club! fan-fiction narrative thousands of times over several months, though even controlling for heavy use the researchers estimate 7 percent of chatbot users engage in fiction generation.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: The concentration of fiction usage among a narrow power-user segment (7% base rate even ex-heavy-use) means monetization strategies for AI storytelling apps should target retention/deep engagement with a niche cohort rather than assuming broad mainstream demand.
insights.quote: But even controlling for heavy use, the researchers estimate that 7 percent of chatbot users engage in fiction generation.

insights.claim: OpenAI disputes the WildChat-based estimate, stating the dataset 'is not a representative sample of all ChatGPT users,' and points instead to a 2025 study by OpenAI and the National Bureau of Economic Research suggesting only 1.4 percent of ChatGPT prompts are fiction-related — though that OpenAI/NBER figure excludes role-play and its erotica coverage is unconfirmed.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: A roughly 25x gap between the WildChat-based estimate (over a third of interactions) and OpenAI's own 1.4% NBER-based figure highlights major methodological disagreement and OpenAI's incentive to downplay fiction/erotica use in its own usage disclosures.
insights.quote: A 2025 study by OpenAI and the National Bureau of Economic Research suggests that 1.4 percent of ChatGPT prompts are fiction-related, a long way short of the researchers' estimate.

themes.theme: Why users prefer AI-generated fiction to human authors

insights.claim: Researcher Melanie Walsh argues AI models offer qualities human writers cannot: they are judgment-free, produce stories instantaneously, and are nearly inexhaustible, which she says is genuinely appealing to a segment of users rather than merely a compromise for lack of access to human-written fiction.
insights.speaker: Melanie Walsh, via Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Identifies specific, durable product attributes (judgment-free, instant, inexhaustible) that AI fiction tools can compete on against human-authored content and traditional publishing, informing product positioning for AI storytelling apps.
insights.quote: There are a lot of qualities of AI models that are different from what human writers have that are actually appealing to at least some segment of users... These models are judgment-free; they can produce stories instantaneously; they are nearly inexhaustible.

insights.claim: Users of AI fiction tools report that a key attraction is unpredictability — the same trait critics call 'hallucination' when discussing factual AI use is reframed as a creative feature by fiction users, who value AI carrying narratives in unexpected directions beyond their original prompts.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili (citing Petra Ferraz de Novaes)
insights.so_what: Reframes 'hallucination,' typically treated as a reliability defect in enterprise/factual AI contexts, as a monetizable feature in creative/entertainment AI products — a useful product-design distinction for AI companies segmenting factual vs. creative use cases.
insights.quote: What fascinates me is the unpredictability... People say that AI hallucinates a lot. But in this case, it's probably what you want.
insights.locator: Petra Ferraz de Novaes quote, opening section

insights.claim: Users like Novaes run open-source AI models locally via a program called SillyTavern to build multi-session fantasy role-plays and self-contained novel-length stories across franchises including Star Wars, Pokémon, and Mass Effect, indicating meaningful consumer demand for locally-run open-source models specifically for uncensored creative role-play.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Demand for local, open-source model deployment for role-play/erotica use cases (avoiding hosted-model content restrictions) is a distinct market segment relevant to open-source model adoption and to hosted AI providers' content-policy trade-offs.
insights.quote: Novaes spends hours at a time building stories with AI, using a program called SillyTavern to run open-source models on her computer.

themes.theme: Erotica and role-play as a specific growth use case

insights.claim: A user identified as Razrien describes using AI role-play, including Google's Gemma 4 model as his current favorite, to generate and interact with hyper-specific personal sexual fantasy characters, valuing AI's ability to serve niche kinks more precisely than existing pornography or published erotica can.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili (citing Razrien)
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that specific commercial AI models (Google's Gemma 4 named directly) are being actively used and rated by consumers for erotica/role-play performance is a data point on informal model quality perception in an unaddressed but sizable use case, relevant to AI companies' content-moderation and model-differentiation decisions.
insights.quote: I have a thing for large, angry women slapping me around. Some models are perfectly good for that... Some models are great at that.

insights.claim: For erotica use cases, AI models let users insert themselves directly into an interactive narrative, described by one user as 'a digital choose-your-own-adventure book but with infinite swipes,' distinguishing it from static published erotica or generic online pornography.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili (citing Razrien)
insights.so_what: Positions interactive, personalized AI erotica as a distinct product category from both traditional pornography and published erotica, implying a differentiated addressable market and monetization angle (subscription/compute-based) versus existing adult content businesses.
insights.quote: It's a digital choose-your-own-adventure book but with infinite swipes.

insights.claim: Researchers suggest a possible future 'tiered publishing system' in which a large volume of AI-generated and self-generated fiction satisfies median reader demand for entertainment, while a smaller tier of human-authored fiction continues to serve a niche appetite for formal experimentation and narrative ambiguity, comparing this niche to the historically small audience of English majors and literary critics.
insights.speaker: Melanie Walsh, via Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: A tiered-publishing prediction implies a bifurcated market structure — mass-market AI-generated content displacing commodity genre fiction, while human-authored literary fiction retreats to a smaller prestige niche — relevant to publishers' and authors' long-term strategic positioning.
insights.quote: English majors and professors, and some people in publishing, have always had kind of a niche interest.
insights.locator: Walsh quote near end of article

insights.claim: Current AI models struggle to produce ornate prose, complex characters, and stylistic flourishes, and fail to maintain coherent narratives at book length, performing best with genres relying on well-trodden story arcs and tropes — but researchers expect these deficiencies to diminish as models improve.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Identifies specific, currently-unsolved technical limitations (long-form coherence, prose sophistication) as the remaining barrier before AI fiction can compete with human-authored long-form work — a concrete capability milestone to watch for in future model releases.
insights.quote: The latest AI models struggle to produce ornate prose, complex characters, and stylistic flourishes, faring better with genres that lean on well-trodden story arcs and tropes. They also fail to maintain coherent narratives at book length.

insights.claim: The publishing industry has already suffered multiple scandals involving suspected undisclosed AI authorship by professional writers, including one publisher canceling a $2 million book deal, another withdrawing a published novel, and allegations that a prize-winning short story was AI-generated.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Concrete, quantified fallout ($2 million canceled deal, a withdrawn novel, a disputed prize) shows AI authorship disclosure has already become a real commercial and reputational risk for publishers and authors, ahead of broader industry AI-use policy standardization.
insights.quote: One publisher canceled a $2 million book deal; another withdrew a novel from the shelves; readers alleged that a prize-winning short story was AI-generated.
